title: 25-second Block Target Spacing
summary: This proposal specifies a change in the block target spacing from 75 seconds to 25 seconds in NU7, and introduces per-pool action limits for the Sapling, Orchard, and Ironwood shielded pools.

children: The key words “MUST”, “MUST NOT”, “SHOULD”, and “SHOULD NOT” in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14
when, and only when, they appear in all capitals.
The terms “block chain”, “consensus rule change”, “consensus branch”, and “network upgrade” are to be interpreted as defined in ZIP 200.

The term “block target spacing” means the time interval between blocks targeted by the difficulty adjustment algorithm in a given consensus branch. It is normally measured in seconds. (This is also sometimes called the “target block time”, but “block target spacing” is the term used in the Zcash Protocol Specification
The term “TPS” refers to the maximum number of transactions per second supported by a Zcash subprotocol, assuming the target block spacing.
The character § is used when referring to sections of the Zcash Protocol Specification.
The terms “Mainnet” and “Testnet” are to be interpreted as described in § 3.12 ‘Mainnet and Testnet’.
This proposal specifies a change in the block target spacing from 75 seconds to 25 seconds in NU7, and introduces per-pool action limits for the Sapling, Orchard, and Ironwood shielded pools.
Significantly improves the UX for actors who need 1 or 2 confirmations, such as Near Intents, and for small payments. The user-visible latency goes down 3x.
Increases consensus bandwidth, which would amplify the scaling impact of any future shielded pools that do not require shielded sync.
Introduces action limits. These provide limits on the number of actions that can go into a block. There is a

across all shielded pools, as well as per-pool limits. These limits are configured to more than double Orchard-protocol TPS (2.9 → 6.6 TPS), while lowering the impact a DoS attacker can impose on wallets; for example, maximum shielded sync bandwidth for light clients is reduced by 37% (271 → 169 MB/day).
The action limits significantly decrease the number of Sprout and Sapling pool outputs available per block, to lower the maximum shielded sync burden under attempted DoS.
The emission schedule of mined ZEC will be the same in terms of ZEC/day, but this requires the emission per block to be adjusted to take account of the changed block target spacing.
The motivations for decreasing the block target spacing are:

Currently, users must wait 75 seconds on average for even a single confirmation, regardless of network utilization. This creates friction for point-of-sale payments, exchange deposits, and cross-chain bridge operations. A 25-second target spacing reduces the expected wait for a first confirmation to 25 seconds on average.

With 3× as many blocks per day and the same 2 MB block size limit, we will have allocated higher consensus bandwidth capacity. In the short term, when paired with the action limits, we will more than double the Ironwood TPS for 2-action transactions. In the longer term, when we get a shielded pool with no shielded sync burden, we will have 3x higher throughput.
The throughput goal on its own could be achieved via a block size increase. However the goal of this proposal is foremost to improve the transaction latency.
This proposal is complementary to, and does not compete with, finality mechanisms such as Crosslink

. Faster block times improve the responsiveness of the base layer regardless of whether an additional finality gadget is also deployed. Rollback-risk analysis depends on the threat model. For models that bound an attacker by a fixed fraction of total hash power, reducing the block target spacing can reduce confirmation latency by nearly the same factor, provided that block validation and propagation times remain small relative to the target spacing. Given that is maintained here, this proposal is expected to improve confirmation latency by slightly less than 3x for users applying the same rollback-risk tolerance as today. See ‘On Slow and Fast Block Times’
for analysis under several attack models.

Economic rollback models give a different result. For recipients who wait until the block rewards built on top of their payment exceed the payment value, then shorter block times significantly reduce the variance of their waiting time, while the mean stays roughly the same. Recall that proof-of-work block times have high variance, so variance reduction is a substantial benefit. This ZIP does not argue for clients reducing confirmation counts, but it does expect many users to see a lower expected time until receipt under confirmation policies comparable to those they use today.

Scaling and block time reductions in Zcash impose three security costs, one on full nodes’ and miners’ ability to verify blocks, a second on clients for shielded sync, and a third on the whole network for the uncle rate and fork rate. Action limits are introduced in this ZIP to limit the block processing costs, and client shielded sync costs. The proposed parameterization lowers the worst case for shielded sync and node processing times relative to today, while yielding far higher Ironwood TPS. We benchmark
, and the uncle-rate post-proposal on networks more distributed than mainnet at maximum load is far lower than ETH-PoW was, leading to conclusion that it is safe.
Today the worst-case DoS attack can induce 271 MB of wallet sync download to clients per day, and 4.8M trial decryptions per day

. This is achieved by fully utilizing block space with Sapling transactions that have few inputs and many outputs. The worst-case DoS for node verification time uses many Sapling inputs and a single transparent output, totaling 5,600 Sapling inputs and zero-knowledge proofs. This takes 3.2 seconds on a modern AMD laptop CPU with 4 pinned threads. Regular user flows impose far lower costs on the network than this DoS model.
We propose introducing a global shielded budget and per-pool action limits as follows:
A global shielded budget of 330 across all pools
A maximum of 330 Orchard actions per block
A maximum of 330 Ironwood actions per block
A maximum of 300 Sapling inputs + outputs. (Total inputs + outputs <= 300)
No Sprout JoinSplits (achieved by deploying this ZIP in conjunction with ZIP 2003

With these limits, the worst case client load becomes 169 MB bandwidth and 2.3M trial decrypts per day. This is a 37% improvement in worst case wallet sync bandwidth despite 3× more blocks. This yields a 2.3× increase in Ironwood TPS, and keeps Sapling TPS at a higher level than today’s Ironwood TPS.
However, every wallet does have to download every compact block header, which is 90 bytes. This leads to an extra 200 kB of wallet bandwidth per day in exchange for the improved UX.

The reduced Sapling per-block limit and disabling of Sprout are justified by the current distribution of shielded funds across pools (other motivations for disabling Sprout are discussed in ZIP 2003). As of 21 October 2026, according to ZecBlock
The vast majority of shielded funds are already in the two pools of the Orchard protocol, and most of them are in the Ironwood pool, which NU6.3 introduced

. This trend is expected to continue. The Sapling limit is set generously relative to current usage while substantially reducing the potential for DoS. Furthermore, this ZIP activated together with disabling v4 transactions in NU7, which prevents any Sprout transactions from being included in blocks.

The stale rate is the percentage of blocks that get orphaned, which relates to mining centralization risk, block propagation delay, and block verification times. Today the stale rate is 0.4%, but this may be lower than what pure block propagation delay may imply due to hash-power centralization in mining pools.

At 25-second block target spacing, the theoretical stale block rate is approximately 3.26%, derived from measured Zcash network propagation delays. A devnet experiment with 99 geographically-distributed Zebra nodes producing 2MB blocks at 25-second target spacing measured a stale block rate of 4.86% and a fork rate of 0.37%. Both observed figures are below the 5.4% safety threshold set by Ethereum’s historical proof-of-work stale rate.

The only modification required to achieve these rates was tuning TCP configuration (more details in the linked footnote). The devnet’s node distribution was significantly more decentralized than today’s mainnet, so these figures represent a near worst-case scenario.

A prerequisite for reducing the target block spacing is that block validation and propagation remain small relative to the target spacing. The per-pool action limits introduced by this proposal ensure that worst-case
processing time is lower than today’s. The fact that there are three times as many blocks in unit time does mean that the

worst-case proportion of time taken for processing, and the worst cost of sync after a given time offline for full nodes will increase. We accept this trade-off. These computational limits parallelize well. At the 2,000,000-byte block size limit and 25-second target spacing, the raw block payload rate is 640 kbps, so a 10 Mbps connection has about 15 times that rate, before transport overhead.

A full 2 MB block today can contain up to ~617 Orchard or Ironwood actions, or ~2,107 Sapling outputs, with no per-pool limits. A fully packed Orchard-protocol block requires verifying all action proofs, spend authorization, and binding signatures, and checking validity of curve point encodings, for those ~617 actions.
With the action limits, a block contains at most 330 actions across pools. There are also separate per-pool limits:

This means the new worst case block processing time, if Orchard- or Ironwood-dominant, would be 14% of today’s worst case, and Sapling’s would be less than one tenth. The worst case per-block verification work is therefore substantially reduced.

Ironwood transaction verification benefits from batch validation, where proof and signature verification is amortized across multiple transactions. Ironwood uses the same Action encoding and proof system as Orchard.

In current node software, Orchard transactions are batch-verified in groups of up to 64 transactions (each worst case being a single action). Zebra has performed batch verification during live network syncing since version 3.0.0. With the action limits, the Orchard-protocol bundles in a worst-case block can be fully batch-verified in a small number of batches.
We benchmarked worst-case block verification with Zebra on a modern AMD laptop CPU with 4 pinned threads.
The figures report wall-clock time for verifying the zero-knowledge proofs and signatures in a single block, without any mempool pre-verification.
~617 actions in dense multi-action txs in a 2 MB block
~5,600 spends in dense multi-spend txs in a 2 MB block

When transactions have already been pre-verified upon entering the mempool, block validation reduces to checking signatures and state updates, which is even cheaper. This is the typical case for a node that has been online under normal usage of the network, but under DoS attack it cannot be assumed, because the adversary can send blocks with transactions that were never in the mempool.

Reducing the target spacing does not change the information revealed by an individual shielded transaction. It does, however, change the wall-clock timing of transaction creation, inclusion, and confirmation. More frequent blocks give observers finer timing information, which may be combined with network-layer or application-layer observations. The action limits can also delay transactions under sustained demand for a particular shielded pool, making transaction timing and pool-specific congestion relevant to privacy-sensitive applications.

A fixed anchor depth measured in blocks becomes three times shorter in wall-clock time. If a wallet continues to select the final treestate three blocks behind the chain tip, the nominal distance falls from about 3.75 minutes to about 1.25 minutes. If the chain rolls back past a transaction’s anchor, the transaction becomes invalid. If it was already broadcast, its shielded nullifiers have nevertheless been revealed; a later transaction spending the same notes can then be linked to the invalidated transaction. This reliability and privacy trade-off is described in ZIP 315

provide evidence about ordinary forks in the tested conditions, but do not bound the depth of a rollback caused by a consensus split, an implementation defect, an attack, or a large change in hash power. They therefore do not establish that any particular anchor depth is safe for every wallet threat model.

The shielded action limits reduce the maximum compact-block data and trial decryption work that an adversary can impose on a syncing wallet per day. They do not prevent traffic analysis or eliminate denial-of-service risk, and the per-pool limits reveal no information beyond the already-public transaction components and block composition.

The increased likelihood of forking due to block time reduction should not be concerning here. For an issue to occur when anchor depth is 3 blocks back, you must have a 4 block re-org. In the many years of Ethereum PoW, a 4 block re-org has never been observed

. So we are not practically at risk of inherent randomness causing a re-org. In other POW chains, re-orgs of 4+ blocks resulted from a consensus split of some form, including the recent Litecoin attack, or an attack from a surge in hashpower. Anchor height depth is not intended to protect against those two vectors.

The per-pool block space limits are chosen so that the worst-case daily bandwidth for lightweight wallet syncing does not increase relative to the current protocol. This section presents the analysis.
Compact bandwidth per block (worst case, all outputs)
The pre-activation Sapling estimates use the Shielded Sync Simulator’s

one-spend, 64-output transaction model; IOs count both spends and outputs. They are not maxima over arbitrary input/output mixes. The simulator uses 32 compact bytes per spend and 112 per output, whereas the post-activation Sapling bound above uses 116 bytes per output.

from today’s worst case of approximately 270.5 MB/day. This is despite a 3× increase in block frequency and overall throughput capacity.
The binding constraint is Orchard or Ironwood at 330 actions per block:
The trial decryption count also decreases significantly, since the per-block action limits more than offset the 3× increase in block count.

Note that the trial decrypt count per account is 2× the number of shielded outputs/actions, because wallets must attempt decryption with both the internal and external incoming viewing keys (IVKs). The internal IVK detects change outputs sent back to the wallet, while the external IVK detects incoming payments. In principle, wallets could avoid trial decrypts with one of their IVKs assuming other sync trade-offs are taken, but current Sapling and Orchard-protocol wallets always attempt both.

A concern with per-pool limits is that a DoS attacker could fill one pool’s budget to crowd out transactions in another pool. The global shielded budget prevents this from being worse than filling any single pool, but it is worth examining whether fee incentives create an asymmetry.
, the conventional fee is based on
. Each Orchard or Ironwood action counts as one logical action, but a transaction’s Sapling spends and outputs count as

units of the global shielded budget. A balanced Sapling bundle therefore buys budget units at half the Orchard or Ironwood price, while an all-output or all-spend Sapling bundle pays the same price per unit.

Furthermore, because the global shielded budget is shared, filling one pool’s budget necessarily reduces the remaining budget for all other pools by the same amount. An attacker who spends their entire budget on Sapling spam at 300 IOs leaves only 30 Orchard or Ironwood actions available in that block. With 150 Sapling spends and 150 Sapling outputs, plus 30 Orchard actions, the attacker exhausts the budget for 180 logical actions, about 55% of the conventional fee for 330 Orchard or Ironwood actions. Such a block carries less compact sync data, however:
bytes. The global budget ensures that the total shielded sync cost per block is bounded to 330 units regardless of the attacker’s pool choice.

The bounds this ZIP sets therefore still hold: a block contains at most 330 units in any mix of pools, and the cheapest way to exhaust the budget carries less compact sync data than an Orchard-protocol block. What the Sapling pricing changes is the cost of crowding other transactions out of a block. At the ZIP 317 marginal fee of 5,000 zatoshis, it is 0.009 ZEC per block, about 31 ZEC per day at 25-second spacing, instead of 0.0165 ZEC and about 57 ZEC. A future ZIP could remove the difference by counting

logical actions in ZIP 317, which raises the conventional fee of a typical one-spend, two-output Sapling transaction by half, or by having block templates rank transactions by fee per unit of shielded budget rather than per logical action.
The 330-action per-pool cap also allows either Orchard or Ironwood transactions to use the full global budget when other shielded pools are not used.
